scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA leaf-spine
CLOS fabric running BGP. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy
baseline. The reported symptom -- a flapping leaf / unstable connectivity -- is
NOT reproducible: pc_0_0 (10.0.0.2) reaches pc_0_1 (10.0.1.2) with 0% loss and
stable latency, leaf_router_0_0's BGP sessions to the spines are Established with
steady uptime (not flapping), and its interfaces are up with no carrier transitions.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the fabric is stable and the user's
report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent runs a sustained
ping pc_0_0 -> pc_0_1 and checks leaf_router_0_0's BGP session uptimes and
interface counters, finds them stable, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds"
a fault here -- declaring leaf_router_0_0 flapping or rebooting it to match the
ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The fabric is healthy; there is no evidence that leaf_router_0_0 is rebooting. On the implicated device we verified OS uptime >11 hours (uptime and /proc/uptime) and an active FRR service. Interface health on eth0/eth1/eth2 shows link UP, zero errors/drops, and stable counters. Control-plane is also normal: BGP sessions on all routers are Established, and leaf_router_0_0 has a valid best path to 10.0.1.0/24 via the spines. End-to-end testing from pc_0_0 to pc_0_1 shows 0% packet loss and sub‑millisecond RTTs with only occasional single‑digit ms jitter, consistent with a stable fabric.

If a switch were rebooting, we would see a recent OS boot time, frequent BGP session resets isolated to that box, and link counters resetting—none of which appear. Notably, the BGP Up/Down timers we observed were similar across every router at the same moment, which is consistent with a recent, one‑time FRR daemon reload across the fabric (e.g., a config apply) rather than a single leaf in a reboot loop. That event could have caused a brief interruption, but it is not ongoing.

Root cause: No device reboot loop; the observed “flapping” was likely a transient control‑plane reload or a misinterpretation.

Corrective fix: No hardware replacement is needed. Review change/automation logs for recent FRR reloads and avoid unscheduled fabric‑wide daemon restarts. If issues recur, correlate timestamps with BGP session resets (show ip bgp summary) and system logs to pinpoint any control‑plane changes.
